cells.remarks: Records the grant of the village Pinapanala by the chief after whom the village was renamed as Allada-Vēmabhūpavaram, to his minister Śrīgiri of Harita-gōtra who is said to have undergone the agni-divya (i.e., fire ordeal) to prove that he and his vargas were not guilty of svami-droha. cells.location: ASSAM, DARRANG DISTRICT, Dekarchuk (P.O. Jamuguri) — Assam
cells.place: Copper plate in the possession of Shri Mahendra Bhattacharjee, received through Shri J. N. Phukan, Gauhati University, Gauhati.
cells.remarks: States that Chao-pha Shü khung (i.e., Svargadev Rudra-simha), the father of the king, granted in Lak-ni Tao-chau (1697-98) 2 gōts of men or paiks to one brāhmaņa Bagish Bhattacharyya of Kaliabar (Ahom: Tung-rung-dām), on the occasion of the dedication of nam khūm Lung (i.e., the Big Tank) at Chemun (i.e., Rangpur), and (owing probably to the fact that the grant somehow went into desuetude) on being informed by Bhattacharyya's son Raghu (or Raghunandan), the king, in honour of his father's words, granted 2 göts of men (names given) to Raghunandan. Mentions the two tribes, Barua of the Bar Chumchi-ring family and Kataki of the Bar Bailong family. (Remarks given by Shri Phukan).

cells.remarks: Records that the construction of the step-well and the garden was started on the given date. cells.place: (Museum No. 25). Findspot: Do.
cells.date: Saka 9[8]2, Särvari, Pushya śu. 15, Sunday, Uttara-yana-Samkrānti= 1060 A.D., December 10. (The samkrānti occurred on December 23).
cells.remarks: Seems to record a gift of land to god Ha[ri*]śchandra dēva (?) by Mahalajā, son of Vanika Gõnaiya. Refers to Jayakēsi of the Manalera family as the feudatory of the king, [Bya]kabbarasi as the wife of the former and Mahāsāmanta Indrakēsi as their son. Registers a grant of land and 30 gadyānas to 12 brāhmaņas of the village for maintaining a satra (chhatra) after laving the feet of 42 mahajanas of the village by Madhukarasa, subordinate of Indrakēsi while the latter was governing Siggāve. Mentions Mailarasa-dandanāyaka probably as the administrator of Bhandivada-grama (Noticed in ASR., 1936-37, p. 98 and SII., Vol. XX, p. xix).

cells.date: Saka 1067, Krōśana (Krōdhan a) Pushya śu. 1, Sunday, Uttar-āyana-sańkrānti. Irregular.
cells.remarks: Recordsa gift of wet-land, a house and an oil-mill for worship and offerings and for the maintenance of a perpetual lamp to god Uttarēśvara by Dēkiyakka, grand-daughter of Rājimayya after performing the pūḍapuja of her lord Jayakēsi dandanāyaka alias Jayadevayya who was administering Tammiyūru and 12 villages as a subordinate of Kadamba Gūhḷadēva. Among the number of other donors who endowed 5 gadyāna each for maintaining a perpetual lamp in their respective names, may be mentioned Rēvakabbe, the dāyi of Dēkiyakka and Chattikabbe, the kiriyabbe of Jayadevayya.

cells.location: AURANGABAD DISTRICT · Tambůru
cells.place: Same slab
cells.date: Saka 1067, Krōśana (Krōdhan a) Pushya śu. 1, Sunday, Uttar-āyana-sańkrānti. Irregular.
cells.remarks: States that when Chattayya was governing the kingdom Ketapayya, the heggade of Māvale-nādu, after offering pādapājā to to Hittimayya, the chief of Tammiyūru and laving the feet of Lākuļēśvara-pandita, endowed 12 houses and 27 mattar of wet-land for the maintenance of the dancing girls of the temple of Uttarēśvara. The donor is said to have paid as kāņika two gadyāņa to the Drodeyas in order to have the endowments made free of all taxes. Mentions Parama-kavi Kannapayya as the composer of the grant and Udayanņa as the engraver. In characters of the 11th century.

cells.remarks: Records the construction of the temple of the goddeas, probably Kshēmāryā (mentioned in verse 2) at Vatākara-sthāna by a goshthi consisting of a number of individuals (names given) including a danseuse named Būtā attached to the temple, while the king's feudatory Rājjila, son of Vajrabhata-satyāśraya was ruling. A certain Satyadēva, son of Pitāmaha was entrusted with the work of construction. The prasasti was composed by the brahmaņa Dhūrtarāśi, son of Divākara and incised by Nāgamundin. Published in Ep. cells.location: BHILWARA DISTRICT MANDALGARH TAHSIL · Achalgadh
cells.place: Stone slab built into the wall of a matha adjoining the temple of Achalēśvara.
cells.remarks: Gives the genealogy of the Guhila dynasty from Bappa down to the ruler, and records that the ruler caused the renovation of the matha on Mount Arbuda, and arranged for the (daily) feeding of four sages there and erected a golden Achalēśa-daṇḍa at the instance of the Naiṣṭhika Bhāva-śamkara, the disciple of Bhāvāgni, who is stated to have been the head of the matha (sthānādhīśa) in earlier times. The record was composed by Vēdaśarman, son of Priyapatu, written by Subhachandra and engraved by Sūtradhara Karmasimha. Cf. Ind. Ant., Vol. XVI, pp. 345 ff.; Bhandarkar's List, No. 610.

cells.location: BHILWARA DISTRICT MANDALGARH TAHSIL · Kankhala (near Achalgadh)
cells.place: Stone slab in the Kankhalēśvar mandir.
cells.date: Vikrama 1265, Vaiśākha śu. 15, Tuesday = 1209 A. D., April 21.
cells.remarks: Records that the Saiva pontiff named Kēdārarāśi of the Chapāla sect renovated the temples of Kōtēśvara and Atulanātha, paved the whole of Kanakhala with large stone slabs, erected probably a highwalled enclosure (around the temples), built two temples of Śūlapāṇi and embellished the temple of Kanakhalā-śambhu by erecting in its mandapa a row of pillars. Also records that his sister Sāntā, described as a brahmacharya-parāyaṇā, built a Śiva temple there. Gives the names of the spiritual ancestors of Kēdārarāśi and mentions the king's feudatory Dhārāvarsha ruling at Chandrāvati with Kumāraguru Pralhadana as the Yuvaraja. The record was composed by Lakshmidhara and (engraved) by the Sūtradhara Palhaṇa. Published in Ind. Ant., Vol. XI, pp. 220 ff.; Bhandarkar's List, No. 454.

cells.date: (1) A.H. 905 (and words)=A.D. 1499-1500, (2) A.H. 947, Rajab 22-A.D. November 22. 1540, (3) Yuzat II, A.H. 1238, Jumādā II, 11-A.D. February 23. 1823.
cells.language: Persian, Nasta'liq (with few phrases in Naskh.)
cells.remarks: States that Mirzā Haidar Gorkan, son of Mirza Muhammad Husain Gorkān, and a grandson on daughter's side of Yūnus Khan, and a son of the sister of emperor Bābūr's mother and brother-in-law of Sultan Abū Sa'id Khan, king of Yärkand (in) Maghulistan (Mongolia), son of Sultan Ahmad Khan, son of Yūnus Khan above-mentioned, was a descendant of Tughluq Timür Khan of the time of Chagghtai, son of Changiz Khan and was born on the first date at Uratappa; that in a particular year (not specified) he set out from Yarkand at the orders of Abū Sa'id Khan and conquered (lesser?) Tibet, and in the same (unspecified) year, on Saturday 4th Sha'ban, along with 4,000 horsemen, he conquered Kashmir but handed it over back to its king Muhammad Shah and returned to join his king then oncamped in Tibet; that he was subsequently appointed to L(h)āsa by the king who himself returned to Yarkand but died before reaching there, resulting in uncertainty in the kingdom, whereupon Mirzā Haidar went to Badakhshan and thence to India to emperor Humāyün; that on finding at Lahore that the latter was fleeing to Iran in exile, he went to Kashmir with 450 horsemen, conquered it on the second date and ruled there for the next 10 years till he was killed by one of the members of the public. It further states that Mirzā Haidar was a widely travelled man, having visited the countries of Türān, Maghulistan, and India and had met great men, was a man of erudition and letters and had compiled the Tarikh-i-Rashidi. It further records that this slab was set up at the instance of William Moorcroft Sahib Bahadur, the chief of the British Cavalry (mir akhur-bashi-i-dault-i-Inglisiya), by Sayyid 'Izzatullah Khan, on the third date. Cf. JASB., Vol. XXIII (1864), p. 283; G.M.D. Şüfi, Kashir, Vol. I (Lahore, 1949), pp. 208-09, pl.

text.remarks: States that Mirzā Haidar Gorkan, son of Mirza Muhammad Husain Gorkān, and a grandson on daughter's side of Yūnus Khan, and a son of the sister of emperor Bābūr's mother and brother-in-law of Sultan Abū Sa'id Khan, king of Yärkand (in) Maghulistan (Mongolia), son of Sultan Ahmad Khan, son of Yūnus Khan above-mentioned, was a descendant of Tughluq Timür Khan of the time of Chagghtai, son of Changiz Khan and was born on the first date at Uratappa; that in a particular year (not specified) he set out from Yarkand at the orders of Abū Sa'id Khan and conquered (lesser?) Tibet, and in the same (unspecified) year, on Saturday 4th Sha'ban, along with 4,000 horsemen, he conquered Kashmir but handed it over back to its king Muhammad Shah and returned to join his king then oncamped in Tibet; that he was subsequently appointed to L(h)āsa by the king who himself returned to Yarkand but died before reaching there, resulting in uncertainty in the kingdom, whereupon Mirzā Haidar went to Badakhshan and thence to India to emperor Humāyün; that on finding at Lahore that the latter was fleeing to Iran in exile, he went to Kashmir with 450 horsemen, conquered it on the second date and ruled there for the next 10 years till he was killed by one of the members of the public. It further states that Mirzā Haidar was a widely travelled man, having visited the countries of Türān, Maghulistan, and India and had met great men, was a man of erudition and letters and had compiled the Tarikh-i-Rashidi. It further records that this slab was set up at the instance of William Moorcroft Sahib Bahadur, the chief of the British Cavalry (mir akhur-bashi-i-dault-i-Inglisiya), by Sayyid 'Izzatullah Khan, on the third date. Cf. JASB., Vol. XXIII (1864), p. 283; G.M.D. Şüfi, Kashir, Vol. I (Lahore, 1949), pp. 208-09, pl.Read more (2 KB)
